papers.title: Evaluation of Machine-Learning Weather Models in Reproducing Mesoscale Tornado-Favorable Convective Environments
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31564v1

summary.one_liner: This paper benchmarks three machine-learning weather models (Pangu-Weather, FengWu v1/v2, FuXi Weather) against reanalysis data on eight tornado-relevant parameters across ten Oklahoma tornado events and lead times of 24 to 168 hours.
summary.plain: Tornadoes form when specific atmospheric conditions line up, such as wind shear and warm, moist air near the ground. This study asks whether newer AI-based weather forecasting models can reproduce those conditions for ten past severe-tornado events in Oklahoma. It finds that performance varies by model, variable, and event: one model does better on a rotation-related measure, another on temperature and moisture measures, though it tends to exaggerate their strength, and forecasts lose accuracy for extremes and fine spatial detail as lead time grows.
summary.why:
Machine-learning forecasts are being used operationally and are much cheaper to run than traditional models, but most were trained on coarse global data that may miss the small-scale conditions behind tornadoes. The paper suggests that headline forecast scores alone can hide model-specific biases and errors in extreme values, which matters for anyone relying on these tools for severe-weather guidance.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Numerical weather prediction (NWP): forecasting by solving physics equations on a grid of the atmosphere.
- Machine-learning (ML) weather models: systems trained on past data to predict the next atmospheric state; much faster to run than NWP.
- Reanalysis: a gridded reconstruction of past weather combining observations with a model, used here as both input and "truth."
- Grid spacing (0.25 degrees): roughly 25 km between grid points, too coarse to resolve many small storm features.
- Lead time: how far ahead the forecast goes (here 24 to 168 hours, i.e., 1 to 7 days).
- Storm-relative helicity: a measure of how much the wind rotates with height, linked to storm rotation.
- Cold pool: a pocket of cool air spreading out from a thunderstorm, often at the surface.
- Overprediction/extreme-value fidelity: whether a model gets the strength of the largest values right, not just the average pattern.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

papers.abstract: Machine-learning (ML)-based weather prediction models have developed rapidly in recent years and are already being used in operational weather forecasting. These ML-based models' performance has exceeded that of traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) methods in certain implementations, with substantially lower computational cost. However, most ML-based models were trained on global data at a horizontal grid spacing of 0.25 degrees, which may be too coarse to capture tornado-favorable parameters. The ability of these ML-based models to predict the parameters relevant for tornado-favorable convection remains unclear. Here, we compare the performance of three ML-based models, Pangu-Weather, FengWu (versions 1 and 2), and FuXi Weather, in forecasting ten distinct convective events associated with strong tornadoes that occurred in Oklahoma, USA. The proposed methodology incorporates five lead times, ranging from 24 to 168 h, for each event and uses reanalysis data as both model input and ground truth. We evaluate the models by forecasting eight tornado-relevant parameters and by conducting spatial and value-consistency checks between model outputs and ground truth. Performance varies across parameters, models, and events. Pangu-Weather performs well for positive storm-relative helicity, while FuXi Weather performs well for several thermodynamic parameters, albeit with some overprediction of magnitude. Increasing lead time is associated with loss of extreme-value and spatial-structure fidelity. In the Global Forecast System (GFS) case study, ML-based models retain convective signals at longer lead times but poorly represent fine-scale structures such as cold pool-like features. These findings indicate that model-specific biases and spatial extremes should be assessed alongside domain-wide forecast scores.

papers.title: Critical ocean physics on the edge of AMOC instability
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31448v1

summary.one_liner: In a 1-degree global ocean model, the authors compute an unstable saddle equilibrium (an "AMOC edge state") that sits on the boundary between AMOC recovery and collapse, and analyze North Atlantic freshwater and heat balances near it.
summary.plain: The Atlantic overturning circulation is a large system of ocean currents that carries warm water north and cold, dense water south, and climate models suggest it may weaken as the planet warms. This paper asks whether that weakening would be temporary or would tip into a collapse that does not reverse. The authors used a global ocean model to find a special, unstable state that marks the dividing line between the circulation recovering and collapsing. They report that near this state, warming and saltiness effects on surface water density roughly cancel out, and that surface density loss lines up with recovery while density gain lines up with collapse.
summary.why: Whether the Atlantic circulation can recover or will tip into collapse matters for regional climate and sea level, so a physical marker of the tipping boundary is useful. The authors suggest the regional net surface buoyancy flux (a measure of how much the surface water is made lighter or denser) could serve as an early indicator, though the text does not test this as a forecasting tool.
summary.background:
- AMOC: the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, a conveyor-like system of ocean currents that moves heat northward in the Atlantic.
- Deep water formation: surface water in cold regions (here the Nordic Seas) becomes dense enough to sink, driving the circulation.
- Buoyancy flux: the rate at which surface water is made lighter or denser by heat exchange (thermal) and by salt or freshwater exchange (haline).
- Tipping transition vs. transient response: a tipping transition is a shift to a different state that does not reverse when conditions return; a transient response reverses once forcing eases.
- Saddle equilibrium: a steady state that is unstable; small nudges push the system toward either recovery or collapse, so it marks the boundary between them.
- Edge state: the unstable state lying on the boundary between the two basins of attraction.
- Global ocean model at 1-degree resolution: a simulation whose grid cells are about 1 degree across.

papers.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is expected to weaken under global warming, but whether this signifies a transient response or a tipping transition remains unclear. Distinguishing between these cases requires a physical understanding of the boundary separating ocean states leading to AMOC recovery from those leading to collapse. In a global ocean model with 1{\deg} resolution, we compute an AMOC edge state -- an unstable saddle equilibrium that anchors this instability boundary. The edge state maintains weak overturning sourced by marginal deep water formation in the Nordic Seas. Analyzing the North Atlantic freshwater and heat balances that govern the edge state dynamics, we show that near the edge state, thermal and haline components of the surface buoyancy flux approximately compensate. Surface buoyancy loss (gain) coincides with AMOC recovery (collapse). Our findings support using the regional net surface buoyancy flux as an indicator for the onset of AMOC tipping.

papers.title: Competing climates of the present-day Earth: from Snowball to Hothouse
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28357v1

summary.background:
- Climate "state": a long-lasting pattern of temperature, ice cover and ocean circulation that a system can stay in.
- Feedback: a process where a change amplifies or dampens the original change; for example, ice reflects sunlight, so more ice cools the planet further.
- Snowball Earth: a hypothesised episode in which ice covers the whole planet, pole to pole.
- Last Glacial Maximum: the peak of the most recent ice age, about 20,000 years ago.
- Ocean heat transport: the movement of heat from warm regions to cold ones by ocean currents.
- Atlantic overturning circulation: a large-scale current system that carries warm water north in the Atlantic and cold water south at depth.
- Coupled model: a computer model that links several parts of the Earth system (air, ocean, ice, plants) so they affect one another.
- Pre-industrial CO2: the atmospheric carbon dioxide level before the industrial era, used as a fixed reference.
summary.one_liner: Using the BIG-MITgcm coupled climate model, which links atmosphere, ocean, ice sheets and vegetation over many millennia, the authors report five alternative stable climate states for present-day Earth's continents, solar output and pre-industrial CO2, and argue that ocean heat transport sets where the ice edge sits in each.
summary.plain: Earth's climate today is only one of several states it could settle into with the same continents, Sun output and carbon dioxide level. The authors ran a long-timescale computer model and found five such states, from a planet fully covered in ice (a "Snowball") to a much warmer one where the Atlantic's overturning ocean circulation has shut down. Each state is kept in place by its own balance of feedbacks, such as ice reflecting sunlight.
summary.why: If several climates are stable under today's conditions, the present one is not guaranteed, which bears on how past glacial-interglacial shifts happened and on the risk of crossing future tipping points. The text does not show how well the model captures real-world behaviour, so these links remain suggestions rather than established results.

papers.abstract: Earth today has one climate, but it could have others. With the same continents, the same solar constant and the same pre-industrial CO2, our planet could settle into strikingly different ones. We explore this possibility with BIG-MITgcm, a model which couples atmosphere and ocean circulation with ice sheets and vegetation, and which can be integrated over many millennia. We find five different climates and describe them here. At one extreme is a Snowball, with ice from pole to pole. A Waterbelt also exists, in which sea ice reaches the tropics and only a thin equatorial ribbon of open ocean survives. There is a Cold world much like the Last Glacial Maximum, a Warm climate in which we live in today, and a Hot world in which the Atlantic overturning circulation has collapsed. Each state is held in place by its own balance of competing feedbacks. Ocean heat transport anchors each climate, holding the ice edge where that transport is weak. The familiar climate of the past 10 thousand years is perhaps just one of several possibilities. This has implications for glacial-interglacial transitions and the risk of crossing global tipping points in the future.

papers.title: Stochastic climate emulation at reduced cost with ACE2.5-ERA5
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28315v1

summary.background:
- Emulator: a fast statistical or AI model trained to reproduce a slower physics-based simulation or observed data record.
- ERA5: a widely used global reanalysis dataset that combines past observations with a weather model to give a consistent history of the atmosphere.
- Autoregressive: the model predicts the next time step from the current state and repeats, producing long simulations.
- Ensemble: a set of runs from slightly different starting conditions or noise, used to express uncertainty.
- Calibrated: the ensemble spread matches how large the real errors actually are.
- CRPS (continuous ranked probability score): a loss function that rewards probabilistic forecasts that are both sharp and accurate.
- Spectral power / wavenumber: how much variation sits at each spatial scale; higher wavenumbers mean finer detail.
- ENSO: El Niño–Southern Oscillation, a recurring tropical Pacific climate pattern that affects rainfall worldwide.
- Spherical Fourier Neural Operator: a neural network design that works on the sphere of the Earth using spherical harmonics.
summary.one_liner: ACE2.5-ERA5 is a stochastic, autoregressive AI emulator of ERA5 reanalysis that adds noise conditioning, a spectrally bottlenecked Spherical Fourier Neural Operator backbone, and a daily time step, yielding calibrated ensembles, improved small-scale precipitation spectra, and cheaper training and inference than its predecessor ACE2-ERA5.
summary.plain: This paper presents a new AI model that imitates the global weather and climate record (ERA5) and can produce many possible future weather paths, not just one. The authors report that its spread of possible outcomes matches its actual forecast errors well from about day 3 onward, that it keeps finer-scale rain patterns more faithfully than the previous version, and that it runs stably for 1000 simulated years. It is also smaller, faster, and cheaper to train, and the team released model checkpoints.
summary.why: Ensembles that are well calibrated, meaning their spread honestly reflects uncertainty, are central to useful weather and climate prediction, and cheaper emulators could make such experiments accessible to more groups. The text also notes that year-to-year variability of global mean temperature is not calibrated in either model, so the approach has a known limit. Broader impact is not established by the text alone.

papers.abstract: We introduce ACE2.5-ERA5 (Ai2 Climate Emulator of ERA5, version 2.5), a stochastic autoregressive weather-climate AI model that produces calibrated weather ensembles with realistic small-scale structure on timescales from days to centuries. Its deterministic predecessor, ACE2-ERA5, retains 36% of its ERA5 target's precipitation spectral power at total wavenumbers 100--179; ACE2.5-ERA5 retains 86%. In weather forecasts its ensemble spread matches its error to within 4% from day 3. Time-mean climate is on par with or better than ACE2-ERA5, the precipitation response to ENSO is improved, and the model is stable over 1000 years. Interannual variability of global mean surface temperature is shown not to be calibrated in either ACE2.5-ERA5 or its predecessor. ACE2.5-ERA5 differs from ACE2-ERA5 in three ways. Noise-conditioned layer normalization, trained with a combined CRPS and spectral energy score loss in place of mean squared error, makes it stochastic. Spectral bottlenecking with grouped convolutions cuts the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator's spectral filter parameters by more than two orders of magnitude and leaves a model a tenth the size of ACE2-ERA5. Its time step is daily rather than 6-hourly. ACE2.5-ERA5 has 3.2 times the inference throughput of ACE2-ERA5. A 6-hourly variant has weather prediction skill similar to ACE2-ERA5. A 4-degree variant reaches comparable climate skill at an order of magnitude lower training cost, enabling rapid iteration during development. We release 1-degree daily, 4-degree daily and 1-degree 6-hourly checkpoints.

papers.title: Carbon dioxide responses shape estimates of Amazon forest vulnerability under solar geoengineering
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26908v1

summary.one_liner: Uses a CO2-dependent forest-sustainability threshold in a shared climate phase space to test whether stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) reduces Amazon forest vulnerability under high-emission and mitigation scenarios.
summary.plain:
The Amazon rainforest may be pushed toward dieback by heat and changes in rainfall. This paper asks whether spraying reflective particles into the upper atmosphere, a form of solar geoengineering, could ease that risk. The authors find it cuts projected warming a lot but leaves substantial drying and longer dry seasons, and the answer on forest risk depends heavily on how much extra CO2 is assumed to help plants.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Solar geoengineering is being discussed as a way to limit climate harm, so whether it protects a major forest matters for policy. The paper's main point is that its conclusion about forest protection swings sharply depending on whether elevated CO2 is assumed to make plants more resilient; the text does not establish how strong that effect is in reality.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI): releasing fine particles high in the atmosphere to reflect some sunlight and cool the planet.
- Solar geoengineering: deliberate efforts to reduce warming by changing how much sunlight reaches or is absorbed by Earth.
- Hydroclimate: the water side of climate, such as rainfall, dryness and dry-season length.
- Climate phase space: a way of plotting different climate scenarios on shared axes (for example warming versus rainfall change) so they can be compared.
- Sustainability threshold: a set of climate conditions beyond which forest is expected to be at risk of loss.
- CO2 fertilisation: plants may grow more or use water more efficiently when CO2 is higher, which is the resilience benefit the paper treats as uncertain.
- Grid cells: the map squares used in climate models; the paper reports the share of these exceeding the threshold.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

papers.abstract: The Amazon rainforest is vulnerable to warming and changes in rainfall, yet whether solar geoengineering can reduce conditions associated with forest loss remains uncertain. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) can offset greenhouse-gas-driven warming without fully restoring regional hydroclimate. Here we assess Amazon forest vulnerability under mitigation, high-emission and SAI scenarios using a Carbon dioxide-dependent forest-sustainability threshold in a common climate phase space. By late century, SAI reduces projected Amazon warming from 5.49 degree Celsius under high emissions to 2.45 degree Celsius, but substantial drying and longer dry seasons persist. Under SAI, 44.7 percentage of analysed grid cells exceed the present-day threshold, compared with 8.7 percentage when the future Carbon dioxide-dependent threshold is considered. This contrast reveals that apparent forest protection depends strongly on the assumed resilience benefits of elevated Carbon dioxide. Our findings highlight the importance of hydroclimatic changes and Carbon dioxide-dependent vegetation responses in assessing the potential of solar geoengineering to reduce Amazon forest vulnerability.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27132v1

summary.background:
- Landslide runout: how far and how fast a slide or debris flow travels after it starts.
- Physics-based simulation ensemble: many computer runs of a flow model with varied settings, used as training data.
- Sparse observations: only a few sensor readings or deposit samples rather than full coverage.
- Latent space: a compressed, simplified internal representation a neural network learns from data.
- Recurrent decoder: a neural network that generates sequences over time from a compressed input.
- NRMSE (normalized root-mean-square error): an error measure scaled to the data range; lower is better.
- Spatial correlation (r): how closely two maps match in pattern, from 0 (none) to 1 (perfect).
summary.one_liner: The paper applies LAPIS-SHRED, a latent-space neural-network reconstruction method trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, to reconstruct the spatiotemporal runout of landslides near Mount St. Helens from sparse sensor data.
summary.plain: Landslides move fast and are rarely watched as they happen, so scientists usually only see the mud and debris left behind afterward. This paper describes a method that rebuilds the full path and timing of a landslide's runout from a small number of sensor readings, using computer simulations to learn from. The authors report that 32 sensor readings from one moment were enough to recover full trajectories with error below 5.8%.
summary.why: Better reconstruction of how far and how fast landslides travel could help hazard assessment where monitoring is thin. The text reports a spatial correlation of 0.843 against observed deposits, compared with 0.853 for the calibrated simulator, so it is close to but not better than the simulator; its practical value in real field settings is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.

papers.title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part II: scale-by-scale budget and mesoscale self-similarity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25829v1

summary.background:
- Deep convection: tall thunderstorm-type clouds driven by rising warm, moist air.
- Self-aggregation: moist convective regions clustering into large dry and moist areas without an external cause.
- Frozen moist static energy (FMSE): a combined measure of heat and moisture in air, used to track energy in the atmosphere.
- Structure function and Yaglom equation: statistical tools that measure how much a quantity differs between two points separated by a distance r, and how energy is transferred across scales.
- Energy cascade: the transfer of energy between scales of motion; an inverse cascade moves energy from small to large scales.
- Power law (r^(6/5), r^(2/5)): a relationship where a quantity scales as a fixed power of distance.
- Boundary layer: the lowest part of the atmosphere, in contact with the surface.
- Part I: the companion paper analysing the same phenomenon in physical space rather than scale space.
summary.one_liner: A scale-by-scale (Yaglom-equation) energy budget of deep convective self-aggregation, finding an inverse energy cascade sustained by boundary-layer production with self-similar power-law scalings of frozen moist static energy and horizontal velocity increments at mesoscales of roughly 100-250 km.
summary.plain: Tropical storm clouds often bunch together into moist clusters instead of spreading evenly, a process called self-aggregation. This paper, the second of a two-part study, looks at how that clustering is distributed across different sizes of the atmosphere, from small patches to large regions. It reports that energy appears to move from small scales toward larger mesoscale circulations (about 100-250 km), with the energy-related variance following a simple power law in distance.
summary.why: Self-aggregation of convection affects how clouds, humidity and rainfall are organised in the tropics, which matters for climate and weather models. The text does not say how directly these scaling laws would change those models, so the practical reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I. We introduce a novel theoretical framework by examining and deriving a generalized Yaglom equation for the second-order structure function $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle$, the scale-dependent variance of Frozen Moist Static Energy (FMSE). Self-aggregation is found to be sustained by an inverse energy cascade driven by boundary-layer production and mediated by mesoscale circulations with horizontal scales $r \sim$(100-250 km). The inverse cascade of energy is found to be realized through a series of shallow and mid-level mesoscale circulations which behave in a self-similar way. Accordingly, the scale-energy variance exhibits an extraordinary collapse across all atmospheric layers onto a robust self-similar power law, $\langle δh_f^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{6/5}$. In contrast, horizontal velocity increments show a degree of self-similarity ($\langle δu_r^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{2/5}$) that retains a residual height dependence. Interestingly, the FMSE scaling breaks down at elevations lower than 750 m and at small local scales below 100 km, allowing us to identify the boundary layer top as a scale-dependent dividing layer where the strong stratification filters the interactions between the surface and free-troposphere, so that small scale dynamics of the low and high atmospheric layers are decoupled while those at large mesoscale are coupled. The derived scaling laws are also used to quantify the moisture-convection feedback via scale-dependent correlation coefficients that show that vertical transport strengthens with scale ($ρ_{mc\perp} \sim r^{2/5}$), while horizontal convergence weakens at the exact inverse rate ($ρ_{mc\parallel} \sim r^{-2/5}$).

papers.title: Approximate Adjoint Models for Memory and Compute-Efficient Online Learning of Hybrid Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26095v1

summary.background:
- Hybrid model: a physics-based simulation with some parts replaced or corrected by a neural network.
- Online learning / calibration: adjusting model parameters while the simulation runs, using errors that build up along the trajectory.
- Gradient: the direction in which to nudge parameters to reduce error.
- Adjoint method and backpropagation through time (BPTT): standard ways to compute these gradients by running the calculation backward through time; their memory cost grows with the length of the training window.
- Truncated BPTT: a cheaper shortcut that cuts the backward pass into pieces, which biases the gradient and drops long-range effects.
- Automatic differentiation: software that computes exact derivatives of a program.
- Lorenz-63 and quasi-geostrophic models: simplified chaotic systems used as testbeds for atmosphere and ocean dynamics.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes approximate adjoint gradient methods (Zero-order and Pullback Reuse) that keep the full-trajectory adjoint recurrence but compute exact pullbacks only at sparse anchor states, to cut memory and runtime when online-training hybrid physics-plus-neural models on geophysical systems.
summary.plain: Scientists often tune computer models of weather and ocean flow by checking how far the simulation drifts from observations and adjusting it as it runs. Computing the correction signal exactly for long runs needs a lot of memory and time. This paper proposes cheaper approximations that keep the overall bookkeeping intact but only do the expensive exact calculation at a few checkpoints, and tests them on three test systems.
summary.why: Training hybrid models over longer and finer simulations is a stated bottleneck for realistic geophysical work, so cheaper gradients could matter for that. The text reports peak memory cuts of up to tenfold and runtime cuts of up to fourfold, with comparable accuracy, but these are the authors' results on three test systems and their wider applicability is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Differentiable programming enables online calibration of numerical models by minimizing errors accumulated along simulated trajectories. This includes estimating physical parameters and training neural sub-models in hybrid configurations. Gradients are typically computed using adjoint methods, or backpropagation through time (BPTT), whose computational and memory costs grow with the length of the training window. This limits the duration and resolution of hybrid-model training, a major bottleneck for realistic geophysical applications. Approaches like truncated BPTT reduces memory use by discarding sensitivities across truncation boundaries, introducing gradient bias and neglecting long-range dependencies. We propose a class of gradient approximation methods that preserve the adjoint recurrence over the full trajectory while approximating only the pullback operators within it. Exact pullbacks are computed by automatic differentiation at sparse anchor states only. Between anchors, sensitivities propagate either through the identity (Zero-order) or through a reused, frozen pullback (Pullback Reuse). This approximation makes the parameter pullback constant within each chunk, allowing the gradient sum to factorize so that a single evaluation per chunk replaces one per time step. We evaluate both on three systems of increasing complexity, an incomplete Lorenz-63 model, a large-eddy closure for two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence, and bias correction in a multilayer quasi-geostrophic ocean model. Peak memory falls by up to an order of magnitude and runtime up to fourfold, with Pullback Reuse staying closest to the exact gradient direction. In all three cases, approximate gradients support hybrid-model training at comparable accuracy, showing that effective online learning does not require exact gradients.

papers.title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23863v1

summary.background:
- Numerical weather prediction (NWP): forecasts produced by solving equations of atmospheric physics on a computer grid.
- Data-driven model: a machine-learning model trained on past weather records (often reanalysis, a gridded reconstruction of past weather) to predict the next state.
- Lead time: how far ahead a forecast is made, from nowcasting (minutes to hours) to subseasonal (several weeks).
- Extreme and record-breaking events: rare events at the tail of the historical distribution, which learned models may rarely have seen in training.
- Verification: the scoring methods used to judge forecast accuracy; the choice of metric can change which model appears better.
- Hybrid systems: combinations that post-process physics-based output with machine learning or couple the two.
- Grey literature: non-peer-reviewed reports, excluded from the formal review.
summary.one_liner: A review of peer-reviewed studies comparing data-driven (machine-learning) and physics-based numerical weather prediction forecasts for extreme and record-breaking weather, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times, with recommendations for more trustworthy evaluation.
summary.plain: Weather forecasters now have two broad tools: traditional computer models that simulate atmospheric physics, and newer models that learn patterns from historical weather records. This review asks whether the newer learned models are also better at forecasting extreme events such as heatwaves, cyclones, heavy rain and record-breaking weather. The authors report that learned models mostly do better for temperature extremes, cyclone tracks and the placement of weather systems, that the evidence is mixed for extreme rain, and that physics-based models still tend to do better at estimating how intense an event will be and at predicting records.
summary.why: Extreme weather is where forecast errors carry the greatest human and economic cost, so whether data-driven models can be trusted there matters for warnings. The paper also argues that headline scores and choices of verification method and case studies can explain much of the disagreement between studies, which is useful for anyone judging new forecasting claims.

papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.

papers.title: Vertical Structure-Based Composites for Analyzing Atmospheric Front Environments
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24260v1

summary.background:
- A "composite" is an average of many similar events, aligned on a common reference, used to reveal a typical pattern.
- An atmospheric front is a boundary between air masses of different temperature and humidity; a cold front is where cooler air pushes under warmer air.
- Fronts tilt with height, so a front line drawn at one pressure level does not match the front at other levels.
- ERA5 is a widely used reanalysis: a gridded historical weather dataset that combines models with observations.
- Thermodynamic fields describe temperature and moisture; kinematic fields describe wind and motion.
- Mid-latitudes are the temperate zones between the tropics and polar regions, where Europe lies.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes vertical composites of atmospheric frontal environments that align data to the actual front position at each height, rather than to a single front line at one pressure level, and demonstrates it on ERA5 reanalysis for 50 European cold fronts.
summary.plain: Weather fronts are boundaries between air masses, and many extreme rainfall events in mid-latitudes happen near them. This paper describes a new way of averaging weather data around fronts so that the averages stay sharp at every height, because fronts tilt with altitude. The authors tested it on 50 cold fronts over Europe and report that the resulting patterns are sharper and more spatially coherent than those from the older method.
summary.why: Extreme precipitation is a high-impact hazard, and better frontal composites could make it easier to study the conditions that produce it. The text presents this as a general framework applicable to different front definitions, but it does not report any link to precipitation outcomes, so its practical payoff is not shown here.

papers.abstract: In many mid-latitude regions, a substantial fraction of extreme precipitation events occur in the vicinity of atmospheric fronts. To understand the processes that lead to such extreme precipitation, it is important to study the environment of the front. In this paper, we introduce a new method for computing vertical composites of frontal environments. Existing approaches construct such composites relative to front lines that represent the front at a single pressure level. However, fronts are vertically tilted and can exhibit substantial geometric variability, both within an individual front and between distinct events. Therefore, at levels away from the reference front line, the alignment of front environments based on a single front line commonly blurs the signals in the analyzed atmospheric variables. Our method accounts for the vertical structure of the front by computing composites relative to the actual front position at all height levels. We showcase the method using ERA5 reanalysis data for 50 cold fronts over Europe and apply it to thermodynamic and kinematic fields. Compared with conventional line-based composites, the new approach yields signals that are sharper and spatially more coherent. It also provides a visualization in which front-relative distances can be interpreted directly throughout the vertical column. Our method offers a general framework to study atmospheric processes in frontal environments and can be applied to different types and definitions of fronts.

papers.title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23429v1

summary.background:
- AMOC: a network of Atlantic ocean currents that moves warm surface water northward and cold deep water southward.
- Monitoring: direct measurements exist only for about the last two decades, which is too short to separate natural swings from long-term climate change.
- Reconstructions: indirect estimates of past circulation strength, built from proxies such as ocean properties recorded in sediments or other archives. Each has debated limitations.
- Tipping point: a threshold beyond which a system changes abruptly and may not easily recover.
- 45°N: the review focuses on latitudes south of this line, where northward and southward flows separate vertically, which makes measurement easier to interpret.
summary.one_liner: A review that compiles heterogeneous observational and reconstructed evidence, focused on latitudes south of 45°N, to assess whether the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is already slowing under global warming.
summary.plain: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a large system of ocean currents that carries warm water north and cold water south, and it helps shape climate. This paper asks whether that system is already weakening because of human-caused warming, or whether that is still uncertain. The authors gather many different kinds of evidence, mainly from the subtropics, and conclude that together they point strongly to a slowdown, though how large and how soon remains unclear.
summary.why: Climate models have long predicted an AMOC slowdown, and a weakened circulation could have large effects on regional climate and carry a risk of tipping points. The text does not discuss specific impacts, so the wider consequences are not established by this summary alone.

papers.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45°N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

papers.title: Why supersonic UAP events are not accompanied by acoustic booms?
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23373v1

summary.background:
- UAP: unidentified anomalous phenomena, reported aerial objects with no confirmed identity.
- Sonic boom: the pressure shock wave made when an object moves faster than the speed of sound.
- Dark matter: invisible matter inferred from its gravitational effects; it makes up most of the matter in the universe.
- Axion quark nugget (AQN): a hypothetical dense lump of quarks (the building blocks of protons and neutrons) and antiquarks, proposed as a dark matter form.
- Quark and antiquark: matter and antimatter forms of the same particle family; the antiquark core is said to supply the energy.
- The paper's central claim that the omega ratio of dark matter to visible matter is roughly equal is a known motivation for the model, not a result of this paper.
summary.one_liner: A speculative paper proposing that a specific class of UAP events are axion quark nugget (AQN) dark matter objects moving through the atmosphere, and that this framework explains the absence of sonic booms during supersonic UAP motion.
summary.plain: This paper tries to explain unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP, the more formal name for "UFO" sightings) by suggesting they are dark matter particles of a hypothetical type, called axion quark nuggets, passing through the air. The authors say the same model explains why these objects make no sonic boom even when moving faster than sound. The text offers this as an argument rather than a tested result.

papers.abstract: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) events have been recorded for decades. However, the nature of these events remains unknown. We advocate an idea that the dark matter (DM) in form of the axion quark nuggets (AQN) made of standard model quarks (or {\it antiquarks}) and gluons could {\it simultaneously} explain many observed puzzling features which always accompany the UAP events, such as high velocity, enormous acceleration, absence of any remaining materials in affected area, etc. This long list of mysterious features also includes the absence of any sound which normally accompanies any supersonic motion. The AQN framework answers this last puzzle as well, which represents the title of the present work. The AQN dark matter model was invented long ago without any intension to apply the model to UAP events. Rather, it was invented with a single motivation to explain the observed similarity $Ω_{\rm DM}\sim Ω_{\rm visible}$ between visible and DM components, which represents a very generic feature of this framework, not sensitive to any parameters of the construction. In this work we use the same framework with the same set of parameters to study the observed UAP events. Essentially we argue that a specific class of UAP represents the close cousin of other mysteries known for decades (even centuries), such as sky-quakes, Ball Lightnings, and Mysterious Transient events. In other words, the UAPs represent different manifestations of exactly the same objects, the AQNs propagating in atmosphere. The fuel powering all these mysterious energetic events is one and the same: it is the antiquark core of the AQNs. We also present some suggestions on type of instruments required to study this specific (and well defined) type of the UAP events.

papers.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18393v1

summary.background:
- Weather forecasting starts from an "analysis": an estimate of the current atmosphere built by data assimilation (DA).
- DA systems typically run in cycles (here, every six hours for global models) and carry a background state forward, correcting it with new observations.
- Ensembles are sets of forecasts from slightly different starting points; calibration means the spread of the ensemble matches how often it is actually wrong.
- Reanalysis is a historical, retrospectively corrected record of the atmosphere, often used as training targets; this model is said to avoid it.
- Microwave sounders and scatterometer winds are satellite instruments measuring atmospheric temperature profiles and surface winds, respectively.
- Limb darkening is the way a planet's brightness varies toward its edge as seen from orbit, depending on viewing angle.
- GSI, GEFS and ECMWF are, respectively, NOAA's DA system, NOAA's forecast ensemble and the European Centre's ensemble forecast.
summary.one_liner: WeatherDreamer is a learned world model that jointly performs data assimilation (fusing sparse observations into an evolving atmospheric state) and multi-hour forecasting end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis targets.
summary.plain: Weather forecasts today start from a "best guess" of the current atmosphere, which is built by a separate, costly system that blends satellite, balloon, and ground readings. This paper presents WeatherDreamer, a machine-learning model that learns to do that blending and the forecasting together, directly from raw observations. The authors report that it beats NOAA's GEFS forecast ensemble for temperature, dew point, and wind out to 12 hours at held-out stations, and that it produces an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU.
summary.why: It challenges the standard split between data assimilation and forecasting, which could make weather analysis much cheaper if the approach holds up. The text reports some mixed results, though: temperature-sounding channels depart from the reference system by up to five times more, so the claim is promising rather than settled.

papers.abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

papers.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21068v1

summary.background:
- Delay-coordinate embedding: rebuilding a system's full state from one measured time series by using time-shifted copies of that series.
- Compressed sensing: recovering a complete signal from far fewer measurements than usually needed, by exploiting structure in the signal.
- Deep learning: neural networks trained on data to learn mappings, here used in the reconstruction step.
- Rogue wave: an unusually large wave arising from nonlinear effects, where many waves reinforce each other.
- Self-focusing soliton: a localized wave packet that can concentrate energy as it travels, governed by the interplay of nonlinearity and dispersion.
- Unidirectional nonlinear water-wave equation: a simplified model of waves moving in one direction, used to describe such dynamics.
- Wave tank experiment: a laboratory basin where waves are generated and measured under controlled conditions.
summary.one_liner: Combines deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity of the unidirectional nonlinear water-wave equation to reconstruct a highly nonlinear wave field from a single point measurement and forecast rogue waves, validated in water-tank experiments.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to predict freak ocean-style "rogue" waves, which can form when waves interact and focus their energy. Instead of measuring a wave across a wide area, the authors use readings from just one fixed point, such as a single wave gauge. They use these sparse readings to rebuild how the whole wave surface evolves over space and time, and then forecast the rogue wave. They report that the forecasts agree well with measurements of the fully developed wave in water-tank experiments.
summary.why: Extreme waves threaten ships and offshore structures, and most sensing gives only sparse data, so a method that works from a single point could matter for monitoring. The text supports the claim only for controlled tank experiments on one class of wave dynamics; its wider use in real seas or other dispersive systems is suggested by the authors but not shown here.

papers.abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.
